subject: english
title: Life (Sonnet by Henry Van Dyke)
subtitle: Sonnet structure (octave + sestet), rhyme scheme, poetic devices, and joyful resilience
curiosity_hook: How can 14 measured lines of a sonnet capture an entire lifetime's journey without rushing past the present or fearing the future?
source_verified_by: AGY Pass 2 Full-Chapter Build (pending human English teacher & rights sign-off)
learning_objectives: Identify the formal features of a 14-line Petrarchan/Italian sonnet (8-line octave + 6-line sestet in iambic pentameter) and trace its rhyme scheme.
Interpret the poet's central attitude toward past losses, future uncertainties, and life's ups and downs using original paraphrased commentary.
Apply textbook vocabulary terms (unreluctant, mourning, veils, crown, quest) accurately in context.

concept_outline.heading: Sonnet Form & Octave–Sestet Structure (p. 18)
concept_outline.summary: Derived from Italian 'sonetto' (little song), a sonnet has 14 lines in iambic pentameter (10 syllables alternating unstressed/stressed). The first 8 lines (octave, rhyming abba abba) state the poet's steady, fearless mindset; the closing 6 lines (sestet) embrace life's winding hills with enduring curiosity.

concept_outline.heading: Core Theme — Present Courage Without Regret or Fear
concept_outline.summary: Henry Van Dyke (1852–1933) contrasts hurried anxiety and sorrow over the faded past against an open, willing ('unreluctant') spirit that pays its fair share to both youth and old age, trusting the final turn of the road to be the best.

concept_outline.heading: Imagery, Metaphor & Coinage (pp. 17–19)
concept_outline.summary: Life is framed through an extended journey metaphor (winding road, rough or smooth terrain, last turn). Key devices include personification (what the future veils), contrast (Youth and Age, rough or smooth, up or down), and the poet's coined adjective 'unreluctant' for emphasis.

key_terms.definition: Willing and eager to act without hesitation (a poetic coinage emphasized on p. 18).
The opening 8 lines (octave) and concluding 6 lines (sestet) that form a 14-line sonnet.
Hides or conceals what lies ahead so it cannot yet be seen clearly.
A sustained, purposeful search for meaningful friendship, adventure, and excellence ('crown').

controls.label: Poem Movement & Perspective Explorer

expected_observations: The octave establishes emotional balance between past and future; the sestet translates that mindset into joyful travel through life's hills.
The opening quatrain follows the enclosed rhyme pattern a-b-b-a (year / soul / goal / disappear).
limitations: Paraphrased commentary and concise analytical phrases only — learners read the full printed poem directly in their Class 10 English textbook (p. 17).

steps.heading: Sonnet Blueprint (14 Lines)
steps.description: 8-line Octave + 6-line Sestet written in iambic pentameter.

steps.heading: Attitude to Past & Future
steps.description: Neither grieving lost yesterdays nor shrinking in fear from what tomorrow hides.
steps.key_takeaway: Live wholeheartedly from year to year with an 'unreluctant' soul.

steps.heading: Lifelong Quest
steps.description: Keep childhood wonder alive—seeking friendship, adventure, and achievement ('crown') on rough or smooth roads.
steps.key_takeaway: Optimism expects the road's final turn to be the best.

question_bank.prompt: How many lines make up a sonnet, and what are its two main parts called (p. 18)?
question_bank.hint: Recall the Italian sonnet structure explained on p. 18.

options.label: 14 lines: an 8-line octave and a 6-line sestet
10 lines: five couplets
options.feedback: 10 refers to syllables per iambic pentameter line, not total lines.

question_bank.worked_explanation: As noted on p. 18, a sonnet has 14 lines divided into an 8-line octave and a 6-line sestet.

question_bank.prompt: What is the rhyme scheme of the first four lines of 'Life' (ending in year, soul, goal, disappear)?
question_bank.hint: Assign 'a' to year/disappear and 'b' to soul/goal.

options.label: a b a b
options.feedback: Lines 2 and 3 rhyme with each other (soul / goal), not alternating.

options.label: a b b a
options.feedback: Correct! year (a), soul (b), goal (b), disappear (a) forms an enclosed Petrarchan quatrain.

options.label: a a b b
options.feedback: Lines 1 and 2 (year / soul) do not rhyme.

question_bank.worked_explanation: year (a) – soul (b) – goal (b) – disappear (a) gives rhyme scheme a b b a.

question_bank.prompt: In the poem's glossary (p. 18), why does Henry Van Dyke use the coined word 'unreluctant'?

options.label: To show he is reluctant and hesitant about growing old
options.feedback: 'Un-' negates reluctant, expressing eagerness rather than hesitation.

options.label: To emphasize a willing, eager spirit ready to embrace life
options.feedback: Correct! 'Unreluctant' stresses cheerful willingness without holding back.

options.label: To describe someone mourning the past
options.feedback: The speaker explicitly avoids mourning disappeared things.

options.label: To refer to a hidden road ahead
options.feedback: 'Veils' refers to hiding the future, not 'unreluctant'.

question_bank.worked_explanation: The poet coins 'unreluctant' to highlight active willingness to meet every year cheerfully.

worked_feedback: Read the poem aloud from p. 17 to hear the steady five-beat rhythm (iambic pentameter) in each line.
Notice how contrasts (Youth/Age, rough/smooth, up/down) reinforce resilience across every stage of life.

flashcards.back: Henry Van Dyke (1852–1933); 14-line sonnet (8-line octave + 6-line sestet).
unreluctant = willing to do something; veils = hides or conceals from clear view.

flashcards.front: What three things does the poet keep seeking since boyhood?
flashcards.back: New friendship, high adventure, and a crown (a worthy prize/achievement).
